talks.title: Can you keep a secret? - An Overview of the OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet's guidance on storing, detecting, and responding to exposed credentials.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the newly published OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet, written by a group of OWASP contributors who often disagreed on how secrets should be handled. The speaker frames the problem with secret sprawl, citing rising counts of credentials found in source code and a supply chain incident in which server-side credentials were reached through a file upload flaw. Less obvious leak paths also get attention, such as pull requests whose compressed or minified diffs can hide injected code, and secrets pasted into tickets or chat tools.

The middle of the talk covers the guidance. Secrets should stay out of code and environment variables, which often end up in logs, and should instead be injected at bootstrap time or loaded into a temporary in-memory file. Storage should sit close to where workloads run rather than being forced into one central platform, with the trade-off of a single point of failure acknowledged. Access should follow least privilege, with generation, rotation and expiration automated. Detection of exposed secrets, including in logs, and regular testing of those detections with a secret scanning tool are also covered.

The closing advice is to prepare an incident response runbook that lets teams rotate credentials quickly and scrub exposed values. An anecdote about a stolen laptop holding over a thousand certificates shows how costly manual rotation can be. The speaker points to the OWASP Wrong Secrets project as a hands-on way to practise detection and encourages attendees to read the cheat sheet and contribute to it.

talks.title: Social Engineering Your Metrics: Using Data Science to Provide Value in Reporting
talks.teaser: Explains which social engineering metrics matter to clients and how simple statistics can make phishing reports more useful.
talks.summary:
The talk starts by reviewing common security metrics, including password length and reuse, breach dwell time and return on investment. The speaker argues that social engineering reports lean too heavily on email opens, clicks and captured credentials, which say little about how an organization actually responds. Stolen credentials, for example, usually point to missing controls such as password policy or multi-factor authentication rather than to individual user failure.

The core proposal is to measure the time between events rather than raw counts. Ratios such as open-to-click show how many recipients move from one step to the next, while distance metrics such as open-to-report or click-to-report show how quickly suspicious mail reaches the security team and where improvement can be measured across engagements. A containment example illustrated the point: when a user who clicked reported immediately, the response window shrank from many minutes to a short interval. The speaker also covered comparing results per client, across sliced engagements and across the full population, along with sample size, mean, median and standard deviation. Regression and cluster analysis were presented as ways to compare outcomes, with the caveat that logs and synchronized timestamps are needed to trace each step.

The closing section made the case that advanced methods such as recurrent neural networks are not required to start. Basic statistics, a consistent program run over time and a clear baseline are enough for most teams. Practitioners were advised to present results to management as a concept of operations, tailor the format to the audience, and remain aware that statistics can be manipulated, so data should be collected and analyzed ethically.

talks.title: Who watches the watchers? - Including ITSM, ITOM, APM, and CMDB in your audits
talks.teaser: Shows how IT service management, monitoring and batch scheduling tools widen attack surface and what auditors should check.
talks.summary:
This vendor-neutral talk argues that the operations tooling most organisations run, including monitoring, configuration databases, ticketing, batch schedulers and automation, is rarely examined closely in security audits. These systems often hold privileged access and a detailed picture of the environment, so an attacker who reaches them gains a map of critical assets and their relationships. The speaker notes that even read-only access to a configuration database can reveal business services, their dependencies and version numbers without the noise of active scanning.

The middle of the talk walks through tool categories. Agent and agentless monitoring, application performance instrumentation that hooks into live runtimes, and real user monitoring via JavaScript injection can all add latency, crash applications when misconfigured, or expose personal data when marketing scripts are added. Trouble ticketing and runbooks can show recurring problems that make new disruptions look routine, and logging levels raised during troubleshooting may never be restored. Batch scheduling and robotic process automation usually run with broad file system, database and ERP privileges while generating few security events, so misuse can blend into normal operations. Patch windows and on-call lists also create openings for social engineering.

The closing guidance is practical. Review service accounts and their rotation, include batch scheduling and automation in audits, log API access with source addresses, and confirm that logging is returned to normal after changes. The speaker also suggests mapping these controls to OWASP SAMM activities and integrating SAMM with ITSM practices where no mapping exists yet, while noting that the work needs dedicated service management staff and closer collaboration with application teams.

talks.title: API Security Through External Attack Surface Management
talks.teaser: Shows how API endpoints fit into external attack surface management, from asset discovery to continuous testing.
talks.summary:
Phillip Wylie argues that organizations cannot protect assets they do not know exist. Penetration tests done once or twice a year leave long gaps, while attackers scan the internet constantly. He defines external attack surface management as the ongoing practice of finding and tracking everything exposed to the internet, and he points out that compliance-driven testing often misses environments outside its defined scope.

The middle of the talk covers the practical side. Discovery starts with IP ranges, autonomous system lookups, regional registry data, and subdomain enumeration, followed by reconnaissance using scanners and open-source sources such as Shodan and company acquisition records. From there the focus narrows to locating web services and API endpoints with enumeration tools, then testing them with fuzzers, intercepting proxies, and API-focused scanners. He also flags risky exposures such as RDP, SMB, clear-text FTP and Telnet, and internal APIs that could leak past the perimeter.

He closes with recommendations: maintain an accurate, continuously updated asset inventory, retest after fixes instead of accepting risk, automate repetitive checks, and review open-source components as part of API testing. The takeaway for a practitioner is a repeatable process for finding forgotten or misconfigured exposed APIs before attackers do.

talks.title: "Who allowed you to do that?" Detecting and Controlling Rogue Third-Party Scripts
talks.teaser: Shows how rogue third-party scripts on web pages can be found, fenced in, and blocked before they steal payment data.
talks.summary:
Brad Burkle opens with the shift to web applications built on third-party JavaScript, where a typical page may load dozens of outside scripts that run with the same access as the site's own code. Browser-side attacks such as payment card skimming happen outside the server perimeter, so web application firewalls and periodic code reviews often miss them. He cites a large retailer that watched a 30-hour Black Friday window and recorded roughly 144,000 attempted data exfiltrations, about 9,000 of them involving sensitive data.

The middle of the talk covers why this persists: fast release cycles, scripts that change without review, and security teams that lack visibility. Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity can help, but they need constant upkeep. The proposed approach is to keep an inventory of every script, watch for changes in behavior, and restrict which page elements each script can read, especially on login and payment forms. A live demo showed a rogue ad script on a checkout page being blocked from reading and sending card details, while the shopper's experience stayed the same.

The closing message is to gain visibility first, then add control, and to prepare for the script-control requirements in PCI DSS version 4. Practitioners should concentrate on the few sensitive pages where scripts matter most instead of trying to police every page at once.

talks.title: Applying Parenthood Lessons to Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Draws parallels between raising children and running security programs, covering containment, behavior change, and leadership.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that parenting offers practical lessons for people who lead security programs. The speaker, a security veteran and parent of twins, uses household stories and humor to make each point. He starts with the idea that silence should worry you more than noise, and he sorts attackers into those that trip alarms, those that leave trails, and quiet ghosts that leave no evidence. Because prevention will never be complete, he stresses containment and rehearsed contingency plans. He also notes that people, like kids, find creative ways around rigid controls and take shortcuts even when they know better.

The middle section focuses on people and leadership. Training alone rarely changes behavior, he says; repetition, consequences and compensating controls do more. He describes an old incident where a taunting message appeared on a reverse proxy, which turned out to be a minor outage with nothing stolen, and he argues that a calm response keeps teams from overreacting. He recommends being present and relatable rather than authoritarian, enforcing policy while allowing limited, reasoned exceptions, and staying firm enough to be respected even when people are unhappy.

The closing points are that problems do not simply get better or worse as organizations mature; they change, so security teams need to adapt their threats and priorities as scope grows. The takeaway for practitioners is to assume failures will happen, prepare and rehearse responses, build real working relationships with the people they need to influence, and stay flexible on policy without giving up enforcement. Resisting change tends to leave security leaders irrelevant.

talks.title: Spies, Saboteurs & Scoundrels: How Russia, China & Nefarious Actors Are Hacking IOT
talks.teaser: Surveys nation-state and criminal attacks on IoT, OT and network devices, and outlines how defenders can discover and secure them.
talks.summary:
The talk opens by framing a fast-growing class of devices, including cameras, printers, VoIP phones, PLCs, KVM switches and building controllers. Many run embedded or Linux-based firmware, speak TCP/IP, and cannot host endpoint security agents, which makes them hard to see and protect. The speaker estimates tens of billions of such devices are in use and points out how many are reachable online with default credentials and firmware that is years old.

The middle of the talk walks through attack stories. These include a military-grade intrusion toolkit leaked online and circulating on torrents, camera hardware shipped with malware preinstalled, a 2016 botnet built on default Telnet logins, and an intrusion that moved from IT systems into cameras, printers and other network gear to steal data over long dwell times. A botnet takedown that targeted PLCs shows that operational technology is also in scope. The speaker shares survey figures on default passwords, end-of-life firmware and critical vulnerabilities, and gives examples of enterprises that could not account for many of their devices.

The closing advice is practical. Build an inventory by talking to devices over their native protocols, since conventional scanners often fail or disrupt them. Track each device's identity and firmware state instead of relying on IP or MAC addresses. Start by rotating credentials through existing password vaults, then harden devices by disabling unused ports and protocols, plan firmware upgrade paths, and monitor for changes. The main takeaway is that credential hygiene is the most achievable first step.

talks.title: Close Encounters of the Vulnerable Kind: A DevSecOps Odyssey
talks.teaser: Maps common security weak points in CI/CD pipelines and explains how to bring security into developer workflows.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how CI/CD pipelines have widened the attack surface and whether security is keeping pace. It begins with the traditional model, where security reviews sit at the end of the pipeline and send findings back to developers, creating bottlenecks. The talk then turns to shifting security left, with checks such as pre-commit secret scanning and software composition analysis placed earlier in the workflow.

The middle section walks through recurring weak points: vulnerable third-party dependencies, with Log4j as a prominent example; static and dynamic analysis tools that bring false positives and blind spots; and infrastructure-as-code files that outsiders could modify. Persistent build servers are contrasted with ephemeral build containers, and the SolarWinds case illustrates how a compromised build server can inject code that then passes signing. Other risks include hard-coded secrets, excessive permissions, missing peer review, rare artifact signing and missing logging.

The closing part argues that culture matters as much as tooling. Suggestions include understanding developer constraints before proposing fixes, supplying concrete implementation examples alongside policy, and building security champion roles inside teams. Vendor claims should be checked critically, and the Cyber Defense Matrix can help map tool coverage and expose redundancy and gaps.

talks.title: Securing Managed Kubernetes Clusters
talks.teaser: Walks through the Kubernetes threat model and practical hardening steps for workloads on managed cloud clusters.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a primer on how Kubernetes is assembled: pods, deployments, services and namespaces, plus control plane parts such as the API server, the etcd data store, the scheduler and the kubelet on each node. It then argues that teams new to the platform should use a managed service rather than build clusters themselves, because the provider takes on much of the control plane's availability and security work.

The threat model centers on three entry points: the API server, the data store and the workloads. The main scenario is an attacker who has compromised an application running in a container. The walkthrough shows how that foothold can reach the instance metadata endpoint, an internal dashboard over cluster networking, and default service account tokens, then escape through a privileged container with host namespaces to the node and its kubelet credentials.

Mitigations include network policies for segmentation, though they only take effect if the network plugin supports them, blocking metadata access, scoping cloud permissions to individual workloads, disabling automatic token mounting, restricting API server exposure, keeping components patched, and enforcing pod security settings. The talk closes with open-source and cloud-native tools for image scanning, runtime monitoring and cluster auditing, along with learning resources.

talks.title: Design-Level Supply Chain Attacks In The Real World
talks.teaser: Shows how design-stage decisions create supply chain weaknesses, with IoT, cryptography standard and influence case studies.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that supply chain security discussions usually begin at coding, dependencies and build pipelines, which leaves the design stage as a blind spot. The speaker defines three kinds of design-level risk: environmental constraints, compatibility and regulation, and malicious influence over decision-making and standards.

For environmental constraints, he uses a low-cost smart switch whose messaging protocol shipped with encryption disabled by default, because the microcontroller had too little memory to run TLS. A later hardware revision moved to a successor chip with more memory, which gave developers room to enable encryption. For compatibility, he traces export-grade cryptography from 1990s export rules to the FREAK downgrade vulnerability, which affected a large share of servers at the time. For malicious influence, he walks through the Dual_EC_DRBG random number generator, which was standardized by NIST and later linked to alleged pressure from intelligence agencies.

He closes with practical remediation: run architecture reviews early, watch internal feature requests so security can weigh in sooner, track errata and upcoming revisions of standards, disable weak options by default, and have diverse experts review standards so influence is visible. The main takeaway is that design choices constrain everything written later and are costly to reverse.

talks.title: FAIR STRIDE - Building business relevant AppSec threat models
talks.teaser: Shows how to turn STRIDE threat models into dollar-based loss estimates using FAIR and Monte Carlo simulation.
talks.summary:
Application security teams often describe vulnerabilities by their effect on systems, while executives make budget decisions in money. This talk presents a way to close that gap. It pairs STRIDE threat modeling with the FAIR quantitative risk framework, expressing threats as estimated financial losses over a twelve-month period rather than severity labels that cannot be added together.

The method splits risk into how often a loss event happens and how large the loss would be, with costs such as engineering time, fines, and public relations work counted separately. Estimated ranges feed a Monte Carlo simulation that produces thousands of simulated years. The result is a curve showing the chance of exceeding a given loss. A live spreadsheet demo shows a parser-level fix lowering simulated losses, so a technical control and a process change can be compared in the same units.

The practical takeaway is that these curves give leadership a baseline and a target they can agree on, and progress can be tracked from one yearly cycle to the next. The speaker argues this helps teams prioritize beyond compliance checklists and makes improvement visible. Feature-level threat modeling still happens separately. Audience questions covered whether the approach suits smaller organizations and how results roll up across many applications.

talks.title: Tips and Tactics for Creating Your Own CTF Event
talks.teaser: Walks through choosing categories, themes, frameworks and challenges for an educational capture-the-flag event.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case for capture-the-flag events as security training. Engineers often click through mandatory awareness modules, while a game can draw volunteers and build trust between application security staff and developers. The speaker compares Jeopardy-style boards with attack-defend formats and favors Jeopardy for education, since players compete against their own learning rather than each other.

The middle of the talk covers planning. Organizers should define the audience's experience level and desired outcomes, then choose categories such as web, forensics, cryptography, networking and reverse engineering. A miscellaneous category can hold non-technical puzzles that keep newcomers involved. A theme and story give each challenge a goal. The speaker compares several frameworks by user isolation, code-checking and scoring options. He warns against challenges that are unrealistic, rely on guesswork, or chain layers that teach nothing, and recommends a written solution and end-to-end testing for every challenge.

For hosting, staff should answer questions patiently, release hints carefully and plan for time zones on longer events. Prizes for many participants, food and a welcoming operations room help. Involving non-security staff and security operations teams can widen participation and add realistic scenarios. The takeaway is that the event is worth running if people stay engaged, the team shows its expertise and participants enjoy themselves.

talks.title: No Code No Risk? What Happens When We Leave No Code up for Grabs
talks.teaser: Explains the security risks of business-built low-code apps, using findings from real enterprise environments and a risk top 10.
talks.summary:
Low-code and no-code platforms let business staff build their own automations and apps, and the talk says adoption inside large enterprises is growing fast, often without security teams knowing. The speaker notes that these tools skip the usual development gates: an app is built and saved straight into production, with little planning, testing or review.

The middle of the talk walks through a top 10 list of low-code risks, based on scanning many live applications across several organizations. Recurring problems include apps running under a maker's personal identity or a shared refresh token that every user inherits, connections sitting in shared default environments, and automations quietly copying email into personal accounts. Other findings include portals exposing entire APIs to anonymous users by default, injection through unsanitized inputs, unvetted third-party connectors, secrets and card data stored in unencrypted databases or written to logs, and abandoned apps nobody maintains. A customer support case shows how a shared admin connection looked like scraping to the security operations team and took weeks to trace.

The closing argument is that these risks are not only the platform vendors' problem, since organizations own what they build, much like the shared responsibility model for public cloud. Practitioners should start by inventorying low-code platforms and apps, finding which connections are shared, and bringing security in early to offer approved patterns that business users can follow rather than only blocking them.

talks.title: Hacking and Defending APIs - Red and Blue make Purple.
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP API Top 10 from both attacker and defender views, mapping each attack to detection and testing.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that APIs are now the main route to sensitive data, and that they often sit outside the controls teams have built for browser-based applications. Scripted clients cannot pass multi-factor prompts or browser profiling checks, and API inventories are often incomplete. Defenders need to know each endpoint's host, path and HTTP method to judge how risky it is.

The middle section follows a penetration testing workflow: passive and active reconnaissance, discovery of how an API is meant to be called, then attacks drawn from the OWASP API Top 10. For each category the speaker shows the attacker's approach, such as swapping object IDs to test broken object level authorization, probing unlisted methods for function-level flaws, or adding unexpected fields to trigger mass assignment. Each attack is paired with its defensive view, comparing posture management, runtime monitoring and testing. Fuzzing, structural data attacks and a brief look at GraphQL round out the section.

The closing takeaways suggest that testers can reuse much of their web testing knowledge but need API-specific tools, while defenders should combine a live inventory, runtime detection and early testing. A community-maintained list of API security tools is also referenced for further study.

talks.title: Automating App Security Tests in Development with Docker
talks.teaser: Shows how Docker containers let teams run web application security scans repeatedly and automatically in development pipelines.
talks.summary:
Gabe Schuyler introduces Docker as a lightweight way to run security tools against web applications. Containers are presented as small, single-purpose environments that start in seconds, can be discarded after each run, and are rebuilt from scratch rather than patched. The opening section makes the case for testing early and often, borrowing developers' knowledge of their own inputs and endpoints, and treating security checks as cheap enough to run on every change.

The live demonstrations launch an intentionally vulnerable web application in a container and point scanning tools at it, including ZAP and Nikto, then move to application-specific tools such as WPScan against a containerized WordPress site. Docker Compose brings up a web server and database together. The talk also shows how exit codes from containerized tools can drive pipeline decisions, how a Dockerfile can freeze a preconfigured attack image, and how parameter lists or API specifications from developers can narrow injection and fuzzing work. Fuzzing with tools such as ffuf is noted as a longer-running option.

The closing part frames this as shift-left security: running the same containerized checks during development, in CI/CD, and even in monitoring, then sharing results with developers. The main takeaway is to start small with one web application in a development environment, add a few basic scans, and grow toward pipeline integration with developer input.

talks.title: Hacking JavaScript Desktop apps with XSS and RCE
talks.teaser: Shows how to audit Electron desktop apps and chain XSS into code execution through node integration, preload scripts and IPC.
talks.summary:
The workshop starts with why companies build desktop apps in JavaScript, citing well-known Electron products, and explains how an Electron app splits into a privileged main process and renderer processes that exchange messages over IPC. It then covers a starting audit: running npm audit for outdated dependencies, reviewing the web preferences in main.js, and running electronegativity to flag common issues.

The middle of the session works through lab applications. An XSS sink assigned to innerHTML is shown to become command execution when node integration is enabled, since injected script can reach Node APIs. The presenter then layers defenses: disabling node integration, adding a content security policy, switching to textContent, and sanitizing HTML with DOMPurify. Further labs cover a preload script running with context isolation disabled, where overriding a built-in function bypasses a protocol check and a file URL runs code on Windows, and a main-process IPC listener that accepts an update URL and leads to a reverse shell on Linux.

The takeaway is to review configuration and dependencies first, treat renderer XSS as a likely path to code execution when node integration or context isolation is off, and apply fixes in layers. The presenter notes the techniques also apply to other desktop app platforms.

talks.title: DSOMM from Theory to Enforcement
talks.teaser: Walks through the OWASP DevSecOps Maturity Model with open source tools mapped to each of its security requirements.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the OWASP DevSecOps Maturity Model (DSOMM) and argues that maturity models help translate security goals into terms leadership can act on. It begins by comparing common frameworks, including NIST's cybersecurity framework, Cloud Security Alliance guidance and OWASP SAMM, before explaining how DSOMM is organised into dimensions, sub-dimensions and up to four maturity levels, many of which borrow from SAMM.

The middle of the talk works through the model's sub-dimensions in turn: application hardening, source control, infrastructure hardening, application testing, consolidation of results, and dynamic and static analysis. For each, the speaker maps the security requirements to concrete open source tools, such as language-specific code scanners, dependency checkers, secret detection, infrastructure-as-code scanning and OWASP ZAP for dynamic testing. Supplier security and some infrastructure controls are presented as more manual work.

The closing part covers the challenge of handling large volumes of findings and describes running checks per pull request so teams can decide what should block a merge. The speaker suggests starting with the early maturity levels and using the model as a roadmap, while noting that the tool choices reflect one cloud-native startup's stack.

talks.title: The DevSecOps Playbook: A step-by-step guide to implementing DevSecOps
talks.teaser: Presents a task-based DevSecOps playbook that spreads prioritized security tasks across development, operations and security teams.
talks.summary:
Paul McCarty opens by arguing that DevSecOps has been diluted by vendor messaging that reduces it to CI/CD tooling with some scanning added. He points to engineers who often deploy straight to cloud accounts, security teams still running questionnaire-driven reviews, and thin operations staff in scale-ups as the persistent gap. He treats DevSecOps as a collaborative methodology built on DevOps, distinct from application security, which he describes as a team focused on code testing.

The core of the talk walks through his open-source DevSecOps Playbook. Its tasks sit in five domains: development environment, source code management, CI/CD and automation, deployment environments, and organization. Each task has a priority from one to three and a difficulty rating based on the people and time it takes. Examples include pre-commit scanning and moving secrets out of .env files. An addendum maps tasks to compliance frameworks such as ASVS, NIST SSDF and Australia's ISM, so common questionnaire items can be answered in advance. He also offers advice on starting a program: map applications to their owners, find willing collaborators, and pick measurable goals.

He closes with the roadmap: a companion document with deeper guidance, more framework mappings, and sorting by priority and difficulty. He invites contributors to the public repository. The takeaway is to treat the playbook as an adaptable checklist sized to an organization's own structure.

talks.title: Defense-in-Depth Engineering
talks.teaser: Walks through design patterns that help web applications survive incidents, prevent regressions, and resist XSS edge cases.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the 2021 OWASP Top Ten's Insecure Design category and argues that defense in depth has to be designed in from the start. The speaker, a product security manager at GitHub, begins with incident response: knowing which sensitive data a system handles, documenting data flows, and agreeing with responders on what to log and how long to keep it. He also covers self-service audit logging for customers and treating every state-changing request as something that must leave an accountable record.

The middle section looks at preventing regressions after an incident. Root cause and variant analysis should turn findings into tests, ideally unit tests close to the logic, with permutations of encoded payloads. Extensibility is next: parameterized queries cannot cover table names, so an allow list enforced by a before filter is a sturdier choice, and insecure exceptions should be annotated so they can be audited. A strict site-wide Content Security Policy with per-page exceptions is presented as a practical way to shrink script-source risk.

The final section covers XSS edge cases that often slip past reviews, including attribute injection, unquoted attributes, WAF bypasses, and HTML-safe opt-outs. Using DOMPurify with default settings is shown to allow many tags, attributes and event-driven behaviors, so teams should learn what their sanitizer permits. The takeaways are to design for incident response, convert incidents into tests, plan exceptions, and understand third-party libraries.

talks.title: Knowing What Risks Matter — And Don’t — In Your Open Source
talks.teaser: Shows how library usage, age, and exploitability data can help teams prioritize open source risk beyond raw CVSS scores.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the pressure developers face to ship quickly, and how open source components make that possible while widening the attack surface. The speaker points to software supply chain incidents such as SolarWinds and dependency confusion, and argues that heavier use of open source raises exposure. Telemetry gathered from thousands of applications frames the discussion.

The middle section walks through findings on library use. Only a small share of the code in a typical application is actually invoked, and many packaged libraries are never active. Libraries are often years old, and the likelihood of serious vulnerabilities rises as they age. The speaker says legacy software composition analysis tools produce many false positives, using a Log4j example where a library flagged on endpoints was never reached. Exposure is compared across Java, .NET and Node ecosystems, and licensing risk is covered, including copyleft and high-risk licenses.

The closing section proposes layering context on top of CVSS: whether a library is active, its age, whether vulnerable code is reachable, and exploit likelihood from EPSS and exploit-chatter trackers. Practitioners are advised to agree triage policies with developers, involve legal teams on licensing, and embed continuous checks in CI/CD so teams address the riskiest issues first.

talks.title: Working through your trust issues
talks.teaser: Shows how the open Dime data format can build application-level trust networks and encrypted messaging between parties.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from public key infrastructure and the two main trust models: the hierarchical certificate authority tree, and the peer-based web of trust used by PGP. The speaker argues that cryptography is hard to get right less because of the math than because developers must pick algorithms, formats and parameters, and that older formats like X.509 and ASN.1, along with JWT's many options and the "none" algorithm, show how those choices lead to mistakes.

The main subject is Dime, an open-source data format and trust module that moves PKI up into the application layer. Its design favours human-readable structures, few decisions for developers, and predefined cryptographic suites, similar in spirit to libsodium. The walkthrough covers how keys are signed and shared in a web-of-trust style, how a root identity issues identities in a hierarchical model, and how a cloud service and an on-premises hub can exchange end-to-end encrypted messages. Responses are cryptographically linked to the original request. The talk also covers clock skew between machines, handled with a configurable grace period, and how suite identifiers let algorithms be replaced later.

The closing takeaway is that trust is effectively granted the moment a new key is first accepted, so that first-use decision needs deliberate design. Expiry, rotation and revocation remain the hard operational problems. The speaker suggests that the security gains of application-level trust can outweigh those costs, and noted in questions that a financial institution is building the format into a two-factor product.

talks.title: Lessons Learned Building a Software Supply Chain Security Team
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from building a supply chain security team, and why SBOMs are only a starting point.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who leads a supply chain security function at a cryptocurrency exchange, describes building that team from scratch over about a year. Coming from application security consulting, they found that supply chain security was discussed heavily at recent conferences but rarely with concrete guidance, and that few tools generated software bills of materials well. The team's scope was defined around open source dependencies, purchased software, supplier risk, and the security of the build and deploy pipeline.

The middle of the talk covers practical findings. Producing a complete SBOM across containers, virtual machines, many repositories and blockchain code proved hard, and many generated outputs failed format validation. Dependency scanners gave inconsistent results, with some Gradle setups silently reporting far fewer libraries than were present. During the Log4j response, locating affected code took days, while a later Apache Commons issue was assessed within an hour after combining scanner output, SBOMs and code search. Personal access tokens were called a major weakness, and suppliers largely did not provide SBOMs at all.

The closing lessons favour pragmatism: start with something small, write down a working definition, expect overlap with GRC and appsec teams, and fit into developers' existing workflows instead of forcing shift-left habits. Collect metrics before launching initiatives so progress can be shown over time. The speaker concludes that SBOMs are a starting point and a bare minimum rather than the end goal.

talks.title: Using your API Specs to attack your APIs
talks.teaser: Shows how public API specs and exposed endpoints help attackers find and abuse misconfigured APIs.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with recent data breaches traced to misconfigured APIs and argues that organisations often leave endpoints exposed without knowing it. The speaker explains why dynamic scanners struggle with APIs: websites expose links a crawler can follow, while APIs need an explicit map of their endpoints. Machine-readable definitions such as OpenAPI and Swagger files supply that map, and they differ from developer documentation written for integration.

Next, the speaker shows how an outsider might locate APIs through public API directories, partner portals, DNS lookups, mobile app decompilation and wordlists, and how a published spec then tells a tool where each route and method lives. Examples include a public GraphQL playground that returned a full database schema through introspection, and a telecom endpoint that disclosed customer details for a phone number. Techniques covered include removing authentication headers and probing low-numbered object IDs for broken object-level authorization, along with the infrastructure, rotating IP addresses and account creation that automated abuse requires.

The closing advice focuses on reducing attack surface: inventory every endpoint and retire old API versions, keep specs internal and behind access controls, disable default admin panels and playgrounds, and generate specs for new APIs so teams can compare live traffic against them. Monitoring outbound response sizes and request patterns can help catch bulk data extraction and enumeration early.

talks.title: The Case for Runtime Protection
talks.teaser: Explains how instrumenting running web applications can block whole classes of vulnerabilities without changing their code.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the argument that application security has made little measurable progress in two decades. Training, policy and developer coercion have not reduced the average number of vulnerabilities per application, and perimeter filtering struggles to tell good requests from bad. The speaker compares this to memory protections such as address space randomization and non-executable memory, which hardened existing software without source changes, and proposes a similar model for web applications.

The middle section walks through the approach. A runtime module loaded with the application inserts checks at dangerous points as the code starts up. Examples included blocking untrusted data from reaching deserialization, detecting SQL injection when user input changes a query's structure, stopping expression engines from launching processes or opening sockets, disabling XML doctype processing to prevent XXE, and blocking reflective access to Java class loaders. The speaker also described observability features that map routes, parameters, access control, libraries and outbound connections, and cited an insurance company case study where most known vulnerabilities in protected applications were covered.

The closing part covered operations and cost. Attack telemetry from inside the application is far less noisy than WAF output, and the speaker estimated lower annual costs for open-source tracking, API security and legacy applications. Runtime protection was presented as a first layer alongside code fixes and perimeter tools, with an open-source YAML rule tool offered for experimentation. The practical takeaway is that teams can spend their effort on strategic issues such as threat modeling and access control rather than individual injection bugs.

talks.title: A visual journey to demystifying OAuth2 and OIDC - why do they exist and how to properly use them to secure your applications
talks.teaser: Explains why OAuth2, OIDC and JWTs exist, how their grant flows differ, and how bearer tokens get validated.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with the problem of letting an application act for a user without handing it the user's password, and of establishing trust between parties that do not trust each other. Everyday analogies, like a parent granting a child a snack or a driving license checked by a police officer, frame authorization as separate from authentication.

The core covers the OAuth 2.0 grant types, including authorization code, implicit, resource owner password and client credentials, and explains why implicit is discouraged since tokens reach the browser. It separates OAuth 2.0 for authorization from OpenID Connect, which adds an identity layer and an ID token. JWTs are broken into header, payload and signature, with a real Cognito token used to show claims such as subject, scope and audience. Refresh tokens are presented as the way to renew short-lived access without repeated logins.

The session closes with bearer tokens sent in an authorization header, and how a resource server validates signature, expiry and scope, returning 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge on failure. The practical takeaway is to use established libraries or managed identity providers instead of building this logic yourself, while still understanding the flows well enough to configure them. Callback URLs and client registration are noted as the hardest part of initial setup, and chained providers such as SAML bridged to OIDC as a frequent source of misconfiguration.

talks.title: How to scan at scale with OWASP ZAP
talks.teaser: Explains how to run the ZAP web scanner across thousands of applications, tuning batching, sessions and false positives.
talks.summary:
Tiago Mendo, CTO of Probely, describes how his team moved from manual web testing to automated scanning of a very large number of web applications with OWASP ZAP. He defines scale as roughly 150 scans a day and explains why they replaced ZAP's built-in crawler with their own, using ZAP only for the scanning step. This creates friction, since ZAP crawls before it scans, batches URLs in ways that can leave threads idle, and needs a separate instance per target for security and resource reasons.

The middle of the talk covers tuning. He explains batch sizes and thread counts chosen by trial and error, grouping URLs by response time and injection points so slow pages do not stall fast ones, and adding dynamic delays so scans do not take targets offline. He also covers session handling, detecting lost sessions periodically rather than on every request, prioritising authenticated and parameterised requests, placing destructive endpoints last, and disabling risky tests that could modify data.

He closes with false positives and resource use. Time-based payloads produced too many false positives, so the team repeated measurements in interleaved waves and extracted evidence to confirm findings. They also filtered low-value informational results, handled disk growth through periodic defragmentation, and used post-processing for their own rules. The main takeaway is that large-scale scanning depends on trade-offs that need tuning rather than default settings.

talks.title: Build more secure apps by harnessing the power of OWASP SKF & ASVS on Kubernetes
talks.teaser: Shows how the OWASP Security Knowledge Framework turns ASVS requirements into labs, checklists and a Kubernetes deployment.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a common gap: development teams are asked to build secure software but have no concrete list of requirements to work from. The speaker proposes the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) as that shared baseline, usable as a testing yardstick, a design guide and a consistent basis for security assessments. Scoping the standard to an application's sensitive data and risk level is presented as the first step.

The middle section introduces the OWASP Security Knowledge Framework (SKF), a platform that wraps ASVS data with checklists, code examples, a knowledge base and containerized labs that each demonstrate a single weakness. The speaker recommends tracking requirements in existing ticketing tools and turning cross-cutting controls into shared libraries or pull request checklists. Deploying SKF was difficult because its Kubernetes configuration predated later API changes, so the presenters patched it and explained a two-cluster design that keeps vulnerable labs isolated from the main application. Scripted deployment on minikube or on AWS with kops and Terraform was walked through, followed by a demonstration of a local file inclusion lab.

The closing advice is to use ASVS as the requirements source, use SKF for training and traceability, and customize its labs and content. The speaker suggested that learning the level one requirements might take a week or two, while implementing them often spans about a year.

talks.title: Fuzzers, analyzers, and other Gophers insecticides
talks.teaser: Shows common Go bugs, concurrency pitfalls, and how static and dynamic tools find them.
talks.summary:
The talk makes the case that Go's easy concurrency model and simple syntax can hide real bugs, and that Go code still shares many weaknesses seen in C and C++. Drawing on security audits of Go projects, the speaker walks through recurring patterns: unchecked or overwritten errors, typed nil interface values that never equal nil, integer truncation on string conversions, slices sharing one backing array, and loop variables captured by goroutines.

Concurrency bugs get their own section: data races, goroutine leaks from blocked channel sends that pile up memory, and missing unlocks on early-return paths that leave an endpoint hanging. For detection, dynamic tools include fuzzing, the race detector, deadlock checks and fault injection, though the race detector misses many concurrency bugs. Static analyzers split into AST-based linters such as gosec and staticcheck, which are quick but noisy, and SSA-based tools such as gcatch, which trace behavior across functions.

A key gap is that most tools ignore third-party libraries, so misuse of web frameworks and ORMs often goes unflagged. The takeaways: combine fuzzing with dynamic checks, run linters for common misuse, use SSA tools for cross-function concurrency bugs, and write custom rules for the libraries a project relies on. A preview of Gotico, an in-development tool for library-specific checks, closes the talk.

talks.title: How To Hack An API In 15 Minutes
talks.teaser: Shows how exposed mobile app APIs and open cloud storage can be found and abused with simple scripts.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the premise that most attackers do not need sophisticated methods. They want a quick win, often within about 15 minutes, against data that is easy to reach. The speaker contrasts this opportunistic behaviour with security researchers who spend long periods on novel bugs. He then walks through a series of mobile app incidents from recent years, where apps exposed APIs without authentication or authorization checks, sometimes leaking entire user databases.

The core method is a repeatable workflow. An app is pulled from a public store and unpacked, and a short Python script extracts the API endpoints it calls. The key step is comparing two versions of the same app, so that only newly added endpoints are tested. These are the least likely to have been reviewed by security teams. Each endpoint is requested without credentials, and a successful response indicates exposure. The same approach is applied to open cloud storage referenced by mobile apps, and hardcoded keys found in app code are ranked by how much damage they could cause.

For defenders, the takeaways are to maintain a complete inventory of APIs, including undocumented ones, to review every unauthenticated endpoint, to keep secrets out of client code, and to audit cloud storage permissions. The speaker notes that mobile release practices often lag behind server-side development, which can leave gaps. In the closing questions, he discusses automating discovery by watching app stores for new releases.

talks.title: No, We Won't Be Threat Modeling
talks.teaser: Shows practitioners how to turn resistance to threat modeling from teams and organizations into gradual, lasting adoption.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses what security practitioners can do when developers, teams or whole organizations say no to threat modeling, whether because they see no value, lack resources or are simply not interested. The speaker lays out the common objections: the process takes too long, feels too conceptual, should be left to specialists, or seems redundant next to scanners and penetration tests. He argues that threat modeling belongs with the people writing code, since they make security decisions continuously during development.

The middle section covers how threat models fail, both when they are never done and after they are produced. Failure modes include relying on a single hero modeler, treating a system's snapshot as a perfect representation, chasing fashionable attacks while missing common ones, and producing documents only to tick a governance box. For getting buy-in, the speaker suggests meeting teams where they already work, such as inside existing design review templates, asking a simple open question rather than handing over checklists, and framing the work as an evolving practice where an imperfect first model still helps. He also recommends offering concrete mitigations packaged with abuse cases that can be turned into tests.

The closing advice is to let each team shape its own methodology, to treat tool output as a starting point rather than a finished report because of false positives, and to measure value by comparing findings before and after design changes. Priorities should rest on exposure and business factors rather than precise risk numbers. Success looks like developers asking questions unprompted, requesting examples, and maintaining a shared repository of models that stays current.

talks.title: Elite Security Champions Build Strong Security Culture
talks.teaser: Presents a maturity framework for building a security champions program that developers actively want to join.
talks.summary:
Many organizations run security champion programs, but few check whether those programs return value for the time and money invested. The speaker argues that security teams cannot grow fast enough to match developer headcount, so champions embedded in product teams must take on routine security work such as reviewing scanner output, adding security user stories and supporting threat modeling. Effective champions need foundational application security knowledge, a genuine personal interest in security, and soft skills to act as agents of change.

The core of the talk is a five-category framework covering strategy, branding, people, execution and measurement, with each area scored from zero to three. The speaker describes a common progression: a grassroots group of enthusiasts, then a mandatory phase where people are simply assigned to the role, and finally a stage where people seek out the program. Practical tactics include getting managers to sign off on champion participation so conflicting demands can be settled early, using existing HR reward budgets, bringing in external speakers for monthly sessions, offering coaching, and scheduling meetings across time zones for global teams.

The talk closes with a suggested target of roughly one champion for every eight developers, illustrated with estimates from companies of different sizes. The practical advice is to assess where your program sits against the framework, then pick a few actions to raise your score over the next few months. The overarching message is to design the program around what champions gain from it, not around what the security team gets out of it.

talks.title: The Abridged History of Application Security
talks.teaser: Traces application security from 1960s password failures and early testing tools through HTTPS, DevOps and modern password hashing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with a 1967 classified United States government review that found software security lacking, then uses a 1938 codebreaking machine as an early example of a security testing tool. It moves through the 1990s and early 2000s, when a network analysis tool, the naming of SQL injection and cross-site scripting, Metasploit and early code review teams turned web testing into a mature discipline. Standards and guides from the OWASP community are presented as widely adopted by compliance teams and large software companies.

The middle section traces DevOps from a 2009 security testing program at Etsy, the first software bill of materials in 2010, and open-source orchestration and dependency scanning tools released in 2013 and 2015. The rise of threat modeling around 2020 and integrated scanning in code hosting platforms show security moving into development pipelines. The HTTPS section follows the origins of certificate authorities, the SSL Labs grading service, Let's Encrypt, TLS 1.3, and browsers defaulting to HTTPS. The password section covers a 1961 password file, a student who printed it, and the path from crypt and bcrypt to Argon2id.

The closing message is that progress is real even when daily triage feels fruitless. The speaker urges practitioners to update their libraries rather than relying on inventories alone, and notes strong demand for application security skills. The future of the field is presented as the ongoing work of the people doing it.

talks.title: Invited
talks.teaser: Explains how security leaders can win support from staff, vendors and boards by using plain language and working alongside other teams.
talks.summary:
Chris Roberts and Charles Valentine open by explaining why Roberts moved from an outside consultancy into an aerospace and manufacturing organization, where he works as the security lead reporting into the CFO. They describe how they began at the company by listening to engineers who had bad experiences with strict security rules elsewhere. Their first changes made daily work easier, such as identity tools with passwordless login and tuned multi-factor prompts.

The middle of the talk focuses on people. The speakers favour short, humorous awareness videos over simulated phishing, and they describe an internal test of two training vendors in which one group's scores fell after training, so they recommend measuring training before buying it. They also urge buyers to question vendors on accountability and to choose smaller partners who stand behind their work. For boards, they advise reporting risk in business terms, such as how many days systems can stay unpatched, and starting with a basic inventory of assets before buying tools. Compliance, finance and IT were brought toward shared goals, and a 90-day plan with clear priorities helped a new security leader get started quickly.

The closing message is that practitioners can change how security is seen by speaking plainly, demonstrating results, and working with engineering, IT and finance rather than apart from them. The speakers plan to return periodically to report on what is working.

talks.title: Hacking Blockchain & Hacking Blockchain
talks.teaser: Shows how Ethereum wallets and Solidity contracts work, then demonstrates a withdrawal flaw and a re-entrancy exploit.
talks.summary:
Marcus J. Carey opens by arguing that security professionals will soon face blockchain payments and assets at their companies, so they need a working understanding of the technology. He explains the basics: an externally owned account is a public and private key pair that signs transactions, gas fees cap how much computation a contract can use, and hot wallets keep keys in a browser while cold wallets keep them on a hardware device. He also covers how apps reach the chain through RPC providers such as Infura, and how a wallet can be generated in code with the ethers JavaScript library.

The middle of the talk moves to development. Carey walks through Solidity concepts, including events that record data on the chain, which he suggests could support chain-of-custody records by storing evidence hashes, and modifiers that restrict who can call a function. He points to OpenZeppelin for standard contract components, the ERC token standards, Hardhat for local testing with simulated time, and Next.js for combined front-end and back-end projects. He also floats the idea of using NFTs as a login credential.

The demos cover common flaws. A contract with no withdrawal function traps deposited funds permanently. A re-entrancy bug lets an attacker call withdraw repeatedly before the balance is reset, and moving the balance update ahead of the external call prevents it. The takeaways for practitioners are to review contracts for withdrawal logic, keep private keys out of source code and in environment variables or secure storage, and test contracts before deployment. The demos ran on a simulated network with fake ether.

talks.title: Indistinguishable from Magic: How the Cybersecurity Market Reached
talks.teaser: Argues that budgets, products and staff have not stopped breaches, and that testing and practice are what is missing.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the observation that the security industry has gained budget, products, training and staff over the past two decades, yet organizations keep getting breached. The speaker frames the gap as a lack of healthy skepticism about how security tools actually work, and as a failure to confirm that purchased products do what they were bought to do. Drawing on a career spanning practitioner, consultant, PCI assessor and industry analyst roles, he walks through examples of misconfigured scanners, an endpoint agent deployed without any policy, and an appliance that never produced a useful detection while consuming hours of manual work.

The middle section looks at how controls get validated. Simple checks, such as confirming that a scanner covered every site on its list, exposed failures that had persisted for months. Breach postmortems, including Equifax and a more recent Uber incident, showed that the causes were mostly process and culture rather than missing technology: an inspection certificate left to expire, a playbook that was never rehearsed, and a detection rule that no one tested. The speaker argues that the intrusion steps in many of these reports look much like a basic penetration test.

He closes with recommendations. Organizations should design a solution to the problem before buying a product, test controls continuously rather than once at deployment, and practice incident response and retrospectives as a team. Security is presented as a shared responsibility across engineering and operations. The main takeaway is to build feedback loops that show whether defenses are working.

talks.title: Infosec is Sick
talks.teaser: Argues that infosec is failing to reduce risk and explains why current scoring and tooling mislead executives.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the claim that information security has drifted away from its purpose of mitigating risk, and that the insurance industry is feeling the result through large cyber claims. The speaker argues that experienced practitioners are moving into management or leaving the field, leaving teams staffed with people who lack solid training. He links this to leadership incentives, where avoiding blame and keeping the board satisfied can matter more than measuring and reducing exposure. Discovering more assets can even increase a security leader's personal liability, which discourages visibility.

The middle of the talk takes aim at severity ratings and letter grades. The speaker argues that these scores do not correlate with real losses and ignore business context, and he uses simple arithmetic to show how a top-severity flaw can be priced far below the cost of replacing a laptop. He also questions averaging grades, which can reward growing the attack surface, and describes web application firewalls as hard to operate correctly and too slow to stop fresh zero-day exploits. On cyber insurance, he notes that insurers often pay claims while customers require coverage, which pushes companies to strengthen their own defenses.

The closing argument is that security should be expressed in financial terms. Remediation cost before a compromise can be compared with expected loss after one, weighted by likelihood and adjusted for company valuation. The speaker admits that existing models such as FAIR are hard to run at scale and that automation is still missing. The practical takeaway is for security teams to frame findings in business value so executives can make prioritization and investment decisions.

talks.title: Drivers for Software Supply Chain Security Programs
talks.teaser: Presents survey findings on what drives software supply chain security programs, who leads them, and how budgets are shifting.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the business forces pushing organizations to treat software supply chain risk seriously. The speaker frames faster delivery demands and growing reliance on software as the backdrop, and contrasts software dependencies with physical supply chains: the concern is the integrity and quality of components rather than their scarcity. Incidents involving a network management vendor, a code coverage tool and widely exploited Java logging flaws show how risk can arrive from many directions.

The core material is a survey of 150 executives at software buyers and 150 at software vendors. Security teams drive initiatives in about 60 percent of buyer organizations, but senior executives are involved in roughly half, which matters for sustained funding. On the vendor side, development operations groups participate more often than security teams. More than a third of buyers reported procurement delays, mostly one to three months, and the speaker argues that changing purchasing requirements has been the most effective lever for changing behavior. Over a third of organizations plan to put at least 10 percent of their application security budgets toward these concerns, mainly on third-party testing and tooling.

For what comes next, the speaker expects software bills of materials to become a baseline rather than an endpoint, paired with matching tools and standards such as CycloneDX and Dependency-Track. Greater transparency is likely to come through standardized assessment summaries, such as those based on OWASP ASVS, and through contract language with remediation timelines. Reachability analysis and exploitability statements can help teams separate real exposure from noise. The practical takeaway is to build an inventory of applications and components, secure executive sponsorship, and ask vendors for evidence in a standard form.

talks.title: 10lbs of tacos in a 5lb bag: Lessons Learned from Security Operations in a Dynamic and Resource Constrained Environment
talks.teaser: Shares lessons from building a security operations function from the ground up at a company mid-transformation.
talks.summary:
The speaker, who previously ran a security operations center for a software company, opens with the threat landscape. Most attacks involve only a few steps, ransomware keeps growing, and ransomware-as-a-service lowers the barrier for criminals. He then contrasts well-resourced security teams with the typical small, stretched team that covers many duties at once.

The core story follows joining a fifteen-year-old global software company during a turnaround, where two people covered thousands of employees and endpoints. Incident response was weak, infrastructure was not centrally controlled, and development and cloud environments were largely unmanaged. The approach started with visibility: identifying key assets, rolling out endpoint detection broadly, and inventorying accounts and existing controls against a framework. Early wins included enforcing multi-factor authentication, automatically installing the EDR agent on new cloud instances, running incident response tabletop exercises, and having finance hold cloud expenses that bypassed security review. A missing response standard was addressed with a 24-hour target for critical issues.

Closing lessons centred on hiring for specific capabilities, planning for self-sufficiency when outsourcing, adopting known frameworks and implementing them fully, and building processes before relying on technology. He urged communicating in terms of business impact and education rather than fear, factoring security into total cost of ownership, and showing progress in phases. He also argued that a defensible decision made through a clear process beats no decision.

talks.title: The Security Practitioner's Guide to Going from "No" to "Whoa"
talks.teaser: Shows security practitioners how to build a risk process that puts acceptance decisions in management's hands.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with what the speaker calls "Atlas syndrome": security staff carry every alert, scan result and pentest finding as a personal burden while leadership keeps deferring fixes. He cites industry alert volumes and recalls a backlog of more than a hundred thousand untriaged scanner findings from his own time running a program. His central point is that practitioners find and communicate risk, but accepting it belongs to the business.

The middle section lays out a practical approach. He recommends anchoring work to a common control framework, running a maturity exercise against a standard such as the NIST CSF to expose gaps, and turning those gaps into a roadmap that management can approve and fund. He argues that severity scores need context, that every employee should be able to log a risk, and that risks should route to management levels by severity for review and sign-off. He compares spreadsheets with a dedicated database-backed platform on scale, joins across data sets and maintenance overhead, and notes that his open-source GRC tool is one option among others.

The close covers building buy-in. He suggests starting with managers rather than teams, framing open risks as problems that need visibility, and reassuring individual contributors that reporting an issue leads to a decision rather than blame. The takeaway is that a "no" is a point to continue from, where partial mitigation, risk transfer or added monitoring can still reduce exposure while leadership owns the choice.

talks.title: Securing the Edge
talks.teaser: Presents survey findings on edge computing adoption, use cases, perceived risks and security controls across six industries.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how organizations are adopting edge computing and how they protect it. It opens by suggesting teams first agree on what edge means, describing it as distributed, close to where data is created and consumed, and software defined. The findings come from a vendor-neutral survey of 1,520 professionals across several regions, conducted with an outside analyst firm.

Three main findings were highlighted. About three quarters of respondents were researching, piloting or running edge use cases in production, with examples ranging from retail loss prevention and factory visual inspection to real-time fraud detection. Deployments remained hybrid, with on-premises and cloud security roughly evenly split. Ransomware was the most cited concern, and patching and network access control were rated least effective, partly because patching was seen as manual and reactive.

The closing message was that security needs to be planned from the start of edge projects, with many organizations putting 11 to 20 percent of their edge budgets toward it and working with third parties. The speaker argued that silos between networking, development, security and business teams are eroding, and that shared responsibility applies to network and cloud providers as well as customers. Attendees were pointed to the full report and industry-specific reports for internal benchmarking.

talks.title: DevSecOps Warning Signs and What to Do About Them
talks.teaser: Outlines common warning signs that a DevSecOps move is stalling, with practical questions teams can use to course-correct.
talks.summary:
The talk questions why DevSecOps often stalls in organizations, noting that security is frequently left out of digital transformation work. The presenter treats DevSecOps as an extension of DevOps and argues that security handled only as risk assessment, without real engineering, slows delivery and leaves teams exposed.

Warning signs covered include security tools used only by a security team, new silos created by a dedicated DevSecOps group, change advisory boards, IT seen as a cost center, deployments taking more than about five minutes so teams batch changes, painful audit cycles, and a lopsided ratio of developers to security staff. Suggested responses include sharing telemetry with developers and operations, building a paved road where security is easy to use by default, and walking each pipeline stage with questions about what is checked, what is published and whether components can be shut off during an attack.

The closing points focus on culture, bringing IT risk and audit into the conversation, and placing security results in the tools developers already use, matched to their workflow cadence. The presenter stresses that the warning signs depend on context, so teams should judge them against their own environment.
